subject: computer-science
title: The Halting Problem and Decidability
welcome_lead: Some problems cannot be solved by any algorithm — ever.
meta_desc: A-Level CS: Turing's halting problem, decidability and computability limits.
final_note: Knowing the limits is as important as knowing the methods.

concepts.def: Deciding whether an arbitrary program halts; proven undecidable.
A problem with an algorithm that always gives a correct yes/no answer.
A problem with no possible algorithm that always halts and gives a correct answer.

Solvable in theory but not in reasonable time as input grows.

walkthroughs.body_html: In 1936 Turing proved that no algorithm can decide, for every program P and input I, whether P halts on I. The proof uses self-reference: assume such a machine exists, then construct a contradictory case.

A problem is decidable if an algorithm answers yes or no in finite time for every input. The halting problem is undecidable. Most interesting properties of arbitrary programs are also undecidable (Rice's theorem).

Even decidable problems may be intractable. Travelling-salesman has no known polynomial algorithm — it is decidable but practically intractable for large inputs. Computability and complexity are separate questions.
